speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise on a matter of urgent and pressing necessity under the provisions of Standing Order 43. In view of the now obvious shortcomings of the government's bilingualism program, which has been documented by successive reports of the Commissioner of Official Languages, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Edmonton-Strathcona (Mr. Roche):
That a select committee of this House be struck to investigate the administration of the bilingualism program and report back to this House its findings and conclusions by the end of 1977.

subsubtopic: PROPOSED REVIEW OF DECISION TO DEPORT MR. PEDRO DENEGRI-MOTION UNDER S.O. 43
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise to move a motion under the provisions of Standing Order 43. In view of the recent decision by the Minister of Manpower and Immigration (Mr. Cullen) to grant political asylum to a Rumanian canoeist who defected at the recent Olympics, and in view of his department's decision to deport a Chilean refugee Mr. Pedro Denegri a former Chilean government official who faces immediate arrest and persecution by the fascist regime in Chile if he is deported, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Nickel Belt (Mr. Rodriguez):
That this House urge the minister to review the deportation decision on humanitarian grounds with the view to allowing this political refugee landed immigrant status in Canada.

subsubtopic: SUGGESTED APPOINTMENT OF COMMITTEE TO STUDY FINANCIAL ADVANTAGES-MOTION UNDER S.O. 43
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, under the provisions of Standing Order 43, I ask for the unanimous consent of the House to move a motion dealing with a matter of pressing necessity.
Considering that all hon. members receive a great many letters from Canadians who wish to take part in the process of renewing our confederative alliance; considering that inconsistent information from governments or organizations reaches us every day in exchanges about the profitability of federalism; and considering that this is a basic matter and that we are now witnessing a polarization of opinions based on conflicting aspects, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Abitibi (Mr. Laprise):
That the House take the lead in this matter of Canada's future by suggesting to all provincial or territorial governments the establishment of an independent non-political committee made up of one or several representatives of each party involved to consider seriously and realistically the future of Canada, the profitability of our federalism and the true desires of all partners in Canada today.

subsubtopic: PROPOSAL TO IMPROVE RELATIONS BETWEEN MANAGEMENT AND THE UNION-MOTION UNDER S.O. 43
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise under the provisions of Standing Order 43 on a matter of urgent and pressing necessity. In view of the fact that the Postmaster General has recently announced to Canadians that another strike in the Post Office would result in the complete dissolution of federal postal services; in view of the fact that recent internal studies of post office middle management indicate that the bulk of the problems in the Post Office originate there, and in view of the fact that even now management in local Post Offices is violating the spirit, if not the

letter, of the collective agreement with Canadian Union of Postal Workers as evidenced by recent strikes in St. John's, Newfoundland, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Sault Ste. Marie (Mr. Symes):
That the Postmaster General immediately undertake to clear up the confusion existing in top and middle management in the Post Office, establish clear lines of authority and instruct management at all levels in the Post Office to abide by the collective agreement between the Post Office and the CUPW.

subsubtopic: MR. DIEFENBAKER-USE OF DEPARTMENTAL STATIONERY TO "SOLICIT FUNDS" FOR GOVERNMENT

speakerposition: Deputy House Leader of the Official Opposition; Progressive Conservative Party Deputy House Leader
subsubtopic: MR. DIEFENBAKER-USE OF DEPARTMENTAL STATIONERY TO "SOLICIT FUNDS" FOR GOVERNMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in the course of the question period today I raised a question in order to obtain from the minister a response and a report as to his investigation into the wrongful use by his parliamentary secretary of departmental letterheads for the purpose of soliciting funds for the Liberal party. I wish to address myself to the response given to me by the minister in the question period.
I do not think the minister went far enough. This matter affects the rights and privileges of every member of this House. As the right hon. member for Prince Albert (Mr. Diefenbaker) said, it is a matter of very serious consequence. Your Honour can imagine an ordinary citizen receiving a letter from the office of the Secretary of State for External Affairs soliciting funds for the government party. Imagine the effect it might have on the ordinary citizen. The practice is not only wrong but it is reprehensible.

subsubtopic: MR. DIEFENBAKER-USE OF DEPARTMENTAL STATIONERY TO "SOLICIT FUNDS" FOR GOVERNMENT

speechtext:
I know not of National Revenue stationery, as suggested by the hon. member, but I know that in this particular case it was External Affairs. What effect would that have on the average citizen of this country? The point that should have been reported on by the minister at this juncture was not only a pure and simple statement by him that it was wrong, but what remedial action he intended. It is not enough simply to say he

did not think it was appropriate; there should be something further.
Is there to be a letter going out to the people who received this correspondence stating that is was a wrongful act? I know Your Honour will want to consider the unfortunate reference made by the hon. member and referred to by the right hon. member. However, the minister has something to answer for if he does not indicate that he is prepared to remedy the situation far more appropriately than he has.

subsubtopic: MR. DIEFENBAKER-USE OF DEPARTMENTAL STATIONERY TO "SOLICIT FUNDS" FOR GOVERNMENT
speechtext: I will be very brief, Mr. Speaker. The conduct of the parliamentary secretary concerned is something that has not yet been touched on. A parliamentary secretary is not an ordinary member of parliament: he is in a position of high responsibility, being the No. 1 assistant to the minister. I am sorry the parliamentary secretary is not here to hear this, or the minister. The conduct of the parliamentary secretary is in question. Had it been a minister who had conducted himself in that fashion, he would either have resigned or his job would have been taken from him. I suggest a similar sanction is a compelling requirement as a result of the dreadful wrongdoing of the parliamentary secretary in this instance. If he did not know it was wrong, he should have known it was wrong.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subsubtopic: MR. DIEFENBAKER-USE OF DEPARTMENTAL STATIONERY TO "SOLICIT FUNDS" FOR GOVERNMENT
speechtext:
The question of privilege raised is a very important one. There was no warning that the matter would be raised today. I think it appropriate that an opportunity be given hon. members to participate in the discussion. There is no urgency in respect of resolving this question on a moment to moment basis, and I would like some time to reflect on the problem.
Initially there are two difficulties which the Chair faces in this situation. First, it is the right of every member of the House of Commons to have the privacy of his own stationery. It is not the function of the Chair, or the administration of the House, to open the mail of a member to determine whether the frank or stationery is being used in a manner that is appropriate or in keeping with any kind of standard guidelines.
This differs, of course, from publications or communications that go out by members at public expense. I refer to the obvious difference with respect to householder mailing where there is regulation because it is being paid for by parliament. However, with regard to a private letter sent out by a member the Chair has no more authority to open that mail, any more than a private individual, whether a member or not.
The difficulty is with respect to the special designations of ministers, parliamentary secretaries or other special offices. That is not a function of the Chair. It is a function of special status which really does not come under the purview directly

of the presiding officer of the House. Therefore, there is an additional difficulty.
In both of these cases it has been accepted that the censure that takes place is precisely the one that is being proposed here. It is not the censure of the Chair, but the censure of the House. Indeed, that is what has been raised. Questions have been raised and questions have been put to the minister. The minister has responded to questions and indicated today that he did not approve of the action. With regard to some pressure for further sanction, I will take some time to reflect on it, but the sanction will be the sanction of the House and not the sanction of the Chair.
In a preliminary way, I do not see the Chair having the authority of interfering with the private mail of any member. Again, I am open to further discussion and to reflect upon it. I think, therefore, the matter ought for a few days to stand over for consideration.

MR. DICK-ANSWERS BY MINISTERS OUTSIDE HOUSE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise on a question of privilege having to do with the answer I received from the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Danson) indicating his intention to make an announcement of a certain program, not inside the House of Commons but outside by means of a press release.
This practice has been objected to on a number of occasions. In the case to which I am addressing myself, for over six months the department has been working to create a youth corps. Such a program was announced in the Speech from the Throne only 12 days short of six months ago. On February 3 a question was put to the Minister of National Defence on the subject, and he replied, "When I am in a position to make an announcement, I will make an announcement." On February 11 a further question on the subject of the youth corps was put to him, and again on February 24, as reported in Hansard under the heading, "Proposed youth corps-Request for details". The minister replied, "I hope to be able to say something within the next couple of weeks." On March 8, in reply to a further question, he stated in part, "I hope to be able to make an announcement along those lines in the near future", and on March 17 he stated, "I hope to make an announcement and answer all the questions by the end of the month."
Mr. Speaker, this is the last day of the month. We were told by the minister on all those occasions that he would be making an announcement. An announcement, in the normal context, is usually an oral communication. I believe the statement which is contemplated is one outlining government plans for expenditures. My information is that an expenditure on the part of the government amounting to between $5 million and $7 million in the initial stages is related to this particular program.
It is my submission that a statement with regard to it ought first be made before parliament because, under the rules, we have the right to question statements on motions, something
March 31, 1977

which is not possible if they are made outside the House to members of the press. I say we are being denied our privileges, we are being denied the right to hear an announcement of this program in the chamber so that we may question the minister with regard to it, and he and his colleagues are denigrating parliament by treating us in this manner. I therefore move, seconded by the hon. member for Wellington-Grey-Dufferin-Waterloo (Mr. Beatty):
That the subject matter of cabinet ministers making statements concerning policy or expenditure outside of the House of Commons, thus avoiding the scrutiny and questions of duly elected members, be referred to the Standing Committee on Privileges and Elections.

speakeroldname: Hon. Barney Danson (Minister of National Defence):
subtopic: MR. DICK-ANSWERS BY MINISTERS OUTSIDE HOUSE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have listened to the hon. member's remarks with great interest. As I indicated in the answer I gave during the question period, I actually hurried this announcement because of my commitment to make an announcement before the end of this month. I welcomed his questions on the program.
It was not possible, between now and the time I got final authority, and certainly having regard to the time I have been away, to provide a statement on motions. In any case, there is no obligation to do so. That matter was canvassed in the course of a discussion reported in Hansard on November 23, 1976, and I draw attention to Your Honour's remarks on that occasion and to other statements on the same subject matter both before and subsequent to that date. There is certainly no disposition on my part to avoid scrutiny of this program or, indeed, of any other of my programs. I want to point out, however, that in this case the hon. member will have the release on his desk this afternoon, when he will see that this is not a program of the Department of National Defence; it is a program to which the federal government is contributing but it is operated by a private corporation outside the public service and the bureaucracy.
Tomorrow morning I shall be quite prepared to answer any questions the hon. member may wish to ask in the House. I feel I have met my commitment that an announcement would be made on the date promised. No information is being kept from the hon. member. As I say, if he wishes to ask questions, he can do so: he can ask all he wishes tomorrow and on subsequent days.

subtopic: MR. DICK-ANSWERS BY MINISTERS OUTSIDE HOUSE
speechtext: On this question of privilege, Mr. Speaker, may I simply say that I concur with all the comments made by my hon. friend from Lanark-Renfrew-Carleton (Mr. Dick). There is one central point at issue here, and it is the right of parliament to hear announcements of policy within parliament. As Your Honour is aware, there is an increasing tendency on the part of members of the government to bypass, to downgrade parliament and make announcements outside reflecting government policies and expenditures. The argument which was put forward by the minister is specious. There could be no more cynical condemnation of the ministerial attitude toward parliament.

speechtext: Let me say, Mr. Speaker, that I am aware of the precedents in this matter and I am by no means suggesting that the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Danson) is in any way discourteous to the hon. member for Lanark-Renfrew-Carleton (Mr. Dick). But that is not the essence of the matter. I share the feelings expressed by the last hon. member who spoke. A lot of work was done by the committee on procedure and organization with respect to the rules. The whole of our procedure was changed in order that ministers could make statements of significance on what the government might be doing in particular areas. It is obvious from the preparations the minister has described that he regards the statement he proposes to make as being at least of some significance. It is, therefore, the kind of statement which ought to have been made in the House for the sake of parliamentary courtesy if for no other reason. He says there is a newness about the scope of this program. It does not come under the Department of National Defence, but involves public funds and private corporations. This is a case where parliamentary courtesy, as opposed to personal courtesy, has been ignored.
We have raised this matter before, but we have not raised it idly. We raised it because we thought the rule was important. I hope that the minister in future would consider this type of conduct, what it does to this place and what fuel it adds to those who are so irreverent about parliament and who say it is becoming irrelevant. Let him consider it from the point of view of the institution itself. I say that without in any way backing away from the strong feeling which was expressed today by the hon. member for Wellington-Grey-Dufferin-Waterloo (Mr. Beatty). It is an important practice and, as I say, we have not raised the matter idly. I am sorry that the Minister of National Defence has transgressed, but I think he owes us parliamentary courtesy at this time.

speakeroldname: Mr. James A. McGrath (St. John's East):

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise very briefly in support of the question of privilege put forward by the hon. member for Lanark-Renfrew-Carleton (Mr. Dick). It is becoming a dangerous and growing practice for ministers to exercise the option, which I grant you they have under Standing Order 15(3), to make statements outside the House while the House is sitting. The minister concerned, the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Danson), has twice this session transgressed in this particular area. This is the second time he has gone outside the House while the House is sitting to make a major statement of policy. The last such incident was when he left the House to fly to Gander en route overseas to make a major statement of policy regarding search and rescue.
I think, Mr. Speaker, that the problem is essentially this, and I realize the dilemma that it poses for Your Honour. The government House leader obviously does not want ministers to interfere with his legislative timetable. Consequently, if it is not in the interests of the government House leader to have a statement made, he will tell his ministers there will be no statements today. As a result, they are made outside the House.
Your Honour will say, and rightly so, that obviously this is an anomaly or a deficiency in our rules, that it is something that should be dealt with by the Standing Committee on Procedure and Organization. Even this rule poses a problem because we have had on the order paper since February 10, under government orders, a notice by the government House leader for such a reference to the Standing Committee on Procedure and Organization. It is obvious that the government House leader has no intention of calling that motion, so it just sits on the order paper. Ministers are able to transgress the rule and, if not the rules, certainly the traditions of the House by contemptuously going outside the House and making major statements of policy when it is not in the government House leader's interests to take up the time of the House.
There are exceptions, I am pleased to say. The Minister of National Defence should follow the example of his colleague, the Secretary of State. He made a major policy statement on the subject of youth in the House a few days ago. Members of the House had an opportunity to respond and, indeed, to ask questions. If the minister had any respect for the parliamentary tradition, he would stand in his place today, under Standing Order 15(3), make a statement and give us the opportunity to respond, as did his colleague the Secretary of State.

speechtext:

Basic agricultural chemicals used in the formulation of pesticides are allowed to enter Canada duty-free although under the General Agreement on Tariffs and Trade (GATT) the duty could be increased up to 15 per cent. speechtext:

subsubtopic: CRTC-WRITTEN COMPLAINTS RELATING TO VIOLENCE OR IMMORAL CONDUCT ON CANADIAN T.V. PROGRAMMES
speechtext:
The
Canadian Radio-television and Telecommunications Commission (CRTC) has submitted the following: 1. Yes, 174 complaints from September 1, 1976 to March 14, 1977.
2.	No investigations were undertaken in response to such complaints. Matters of violence or alleged immoral conduct are an aspect of programming. Under the Broadcasting Act "all persons licensed to carry on broadcasting undertakings have a responsibility for programmes they broadcast...". As a consequence, complaints from the listening or viewing public which the Commission receives are sent to the licensee by the Commission, requesting that the licensee respond to the writer setting forth how he, the licensee, sees his responsibilities in connection with programming of this nature. The commission is not a censor. It expects the licensee to be responsible for the programming broadcast and it is regular commission practice to examine each licensee at public hearings for the renewal of a licence, in connection with the programmes they broadcast. Direct intervention in the programming of Canadian television licensees by the commission is not authorized under the Broadcasting Act. Such intervention to prohibit or control violent or immoral scenes could only be accomplished through new legislative action by Parliament.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO ESTABLISH DEPARTMENT OF EMPLOYMENT AND IMMIGRATION, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in the few remarks I was able to make yesterday afternoon I mentioned the speech delivered by the hon. member for South Western Nova (Miss Campbell). I intend to make some further comments on that speech, but prior to doing so I should like to make some general remarks about the legislation in question as well as the new responsibilities that will be assumed by the Minister of Manpower and Immigration (Mr. Cullen) who will become minister of employment under the legislation.
First of all, I should like to say to the minister that I support the objectives contained in the legislation from the point of view that I believe it is a realistic proposition once again to unite the manpower operations of the government with the unemployment operations of the government as it has existed for many years. From that point of view, I think it is only fair to say to the minister that in a personal way I have found a tremendous burden has been placed upon members of the

Manpower operation and the Unemployment Insurance Commission since the time the legislation that we are now amending was passed.
I think my experience is not unique. It is no different from that faced by many members across the country through the tremendous increase in the workload of our offices as a result of the amended act. This has happened for a number of reasons, the first being that the former unemployment insurance legislation was in place for a very long time and therefore the work force understood it. Suddenly there was new legislation that carried with it many aspects which were not clearly understood by the work force and, as a result, there were many problems. I think these problems were tremendously worsened by the fact that the UIC was computerized at about the same time and there were many breakdowns and things of that nature.
I think the minister and his employees should know that we appreciate the tremendous amount of hard work done by people in the Unemployment Insurance Commission. They have done everything they can to eliminate the many problems which have developed. There is no doubt that workers were not used to computer cards when completing their claims and many problems were created in that way, and also from a public relations point of view. The staff of the Unemployment Insurance Commission, with some exceptions, did a tremendous job in reacting to the problems faced by unemployed workers. For this they deserve a pat on the back, rather than a kick in the pants as we are so often inclined to give them, because this or that particular situation makes people upset.
Through my office I am in daily contact with the Unemployment Insurance Commission, and I find that if there is any way they can shorten the route to the resolution of a problem, they will use it. I believe they deserve credit and they should be told by the minister, on behalf of members of this House, that we appreciate the co-operation they give our staffs in trying to solve problems. I think we are very fortunate to have this minister at the present time.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO ESTABLISH DEPARTMENT OF EMPLOYMENT AND IMMIGRATION, ETC.
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO ESTABLISH DEPARTMENT OF EMPLOYMENT AND IMMIGRATION, ETC.
speechtext: From the point of view that whether as a backbencher, a parliamentary secretary or whatever, I have always found him co-operative.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO ESTABLISH DEPARTMENT OF EMPLOYMENT AND IMMIGRATION, ETC.
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO ESTABLISH DEPARTMENT OF EMPLOYMENT AND IMMIGRATION, ETC.
speechtext:
I think the government could not have been more unkind to him however, than in trying to put this legislation through the House at this time. A year ago I anticipated that the government would move in this direction because it was obvious that the Unemployment Insurance Commission was getting well beyond an insurance scheme and was becoming more of a welfare scheme. It was obvious that something had to be done to get control of the situation and put in place a scheme that was more insurance than welfare. The Canada Assistance Plan is available to look after the welfare needs of our society which are very much a burden on many people who want to work today and cannot find jobs.
March 31, 1977

From that point of view I asked my constituents whether they believed the period for qualification should be extended. A considerable number of them indicated that they believed, as we believed when the original legislation was before the House, that there should be a longer qualification period. So it would not be reasonable for me now to say to the minister that I do not believe in the concept of extending from 8 to 12 weeks the period for qualification, but I do think it is very difficult for any member of the House, in view of the fact that close to one million people are unemployed in this country, to try to take any type of action that may result in the disqualification of people who are now qualified to receive benefits, or to put an individual in a more difficult position when there are not sufficient jobs available to secure a job.
I understand there are some 13 members in the minister's own party who have expressed deep concern over the extension of the qualification period from 8 to 12 weeks. I have heard the minister say that he is concerned about that, that he is flexible. I do not know how flexible he is. The minister has been informed by our party that we intend to move some amendments in committee which will reflect the concern that all members have about this matter, and I hope that serious consideration will be given to this situation because I believe that what the minister is endeavouring to do is right. But I also believe we must give serious thought to the heavy unemployment situation in our country at this time. We should be able to find a compromise at least for a period of time until we overcome the problem. So it pleases me to know that the minister is at least giving serious consideration to this problem and is not so determined or intransigent to just give us this legislation and say, "You can take it or lump it, whatever you want".
One of the things that, unfortunately, is associated with Standing Order 75C is the fact that the type of legislation it encompasses poisons the air and eliminates some willingness, on the part of some hon. members at least, to be as co-operative as they might otherwise be. I understand that there are timetables to be met and things of that nature. I am just sorry that a closure motion has to be imposed on this piece of legislation, because to a degree it eliminates the spirit of co-operation that would exist otherwise.
One of the things that has concerned me about the debate- and it is an understandable problem-is the fact that we are debating, in respect of this piece of legislation, an insurance scheme. We are not really debating problems associated with the malaise that is in the economy at present. I hope that when the Minister of Finance (Mr. Macdonald) brings in his budget tonight, that malaise will be eliminated at least to a degree and, there will be a softening of the hard attitude of the government with regard to the unemployment situation. But while I appreciate it is hard to separate the two, what we have to look at is the fact that we are indirectly taxing the Canadian nation an excessive amount because the scheme, in its present form-which will be changed with this legislation-is not capable of paying the bills. We have to work out, if we are
Employment and Immigration
going to eliminate some of the pull that we have on the money markets, some of the problem areas that exist in the Unemployment Insurance Act because of the extent of unemployment.
The minister has always been a very helpful supporter of the scheme to harness Fundy tidal power. Throughout the period of time that he has been in the House he has endeavoured to associate himself with the Atlantic provinces as often as he could. I am sure he appreciates the extent of unemployment and the terrible problems we are facing throughout the area. For instance, in my constituency the town of Truro has always had one of the healthiest economic bases of any town in the maritime provinces. But now it is in grave difficulty. It has an unemployment rate of close to 20 per cent. It is hard to believe, because it has so many industries and there is so much diversification of industry there.
My home town of Amherst usually reflects the economy of the area, but Truro has always been an area with a very low unemployment rate. However, that is not the case at present. I am only saying that to impress upon the minister, as the minister of manpower or as the minister of employment, as he will become, that he should put some extra push behind a project like the Fundy tidal project in the days ahead, because I know he realizes the potential of that project, he realizes what it will do for employment in the maritime provinces and that it is the kind of project that will revitalize the economy of the area as well as partly solve the difficult energy problem we face there. So I hope the minister will do his level best to see that that project is given an increased impetus in the days ahead in the hope that we can get it on the rails and provide the jobs that the people require.
While I am anxious to bring to the minister's attention the good work that his officials do so far as I am concerned in my daily discussions with them, situations occur from time to time which, I believe, merit special consideration. I have a constituent by the name of Lloyd D. Gilroy who has been disqualified from unemployment benefits. The situation has now reached the point where he has had to hire a lawyer. That lawyer made a request to have the case submitted to an umpire. I received a letter from the lawyer, Larry A. McKim, Mr. Gilroy's solicitor, who informs me of this fact. 1 am pointing this out because I think it is important that the minister's officials think very carefully, especially at a time of high unemployment, before making certain decisions which may result in a disqualification by deceiving the individual whom they are interviewing, whether they are doing this intentionally or because they feel the person is not making a real effort to secure employment for himself or herself.
In his letter, Mr. McKim wrote the following:
Two things about this case bother me a lot, I guess because both seem contrary to natural justice. One is the trickery of "getting" one to refuse a job which doesn't exist (alleged labourer's job in Springhill) and the other dealing with the UIC's not adequately, if at all, stressing to the claimant the principle as set forth in the letter from George Lambert, departmental assistant, to you dated March 5, 1977, "... That if a claimant is still unemployed after a reasonable

March 31, 1977
Employment and Immigration
period of time has passed, it is expected that he should broaden the area of his search for work and relax the restrictions on the type of job he would accept. If he does not do so, he cannot be considered fully available for work and benefits are suspended". As to this principle, it seems to be sacred unto the UIC people, who apparently do all the interpreting of the phrases ''reasonable time", "broaden the area of his search", and "relax the restrictions". The trick is to let the claimant delimit himself for a while, within the so-called principles, and then inject some new principles into the game, something like coming up with a ground-rule double after a hitter has run all the way from home to third.
From time to time I encounter these situations, and usually after discussion with the claimant so that he fully understands his responsibilities with respect to seeking employment and after talking with the insurance officer, the problem is solved. I have talked to the gentleman involved in this particular case on a number of occasions, and it upsets me that an insurance officer will take a position which makes it impossible for a person to be able to seek employment in the area in which he feels he should be seeking it. For instance, in this particular case the gentleman in question had just purchased a new home in the area where he had been working. It was suggested that he go a distance from one area of close to 70 miles and from another area of close to 50 miles to work. That person just happened to purchase a home, and it was impossible for him to do that. When insurance officers enlarge the scope, they sometimes can create inequities or, as Mr. McKim puts it, they can eliminate natural justice with respect to what insurance officers know people can do.
I put this particular case before the minister because I think the individual was treated unfairly. I do not think the minister or the UIC want anyone to be treated unfairly. The objective is to see that people who are receiving unemployment insurance benefits are entitled to them. In the past six or eight months there has been a tremendous difference in the operations of the UIC with respect to eliminating people who formerly took advantage of the fund and secured benefits to which they were really not entitled.
I feel that the work force has displayed a different attitude. As long as a person knows his chum is getting benefits to which he is not entitled, he almost feels he is entitled to the same thing. However, when he discovers that his chum is suspended from receiving benefits or is prosecuted and faces severe penalties by way of the elimination of benefits and the paying back of substantial portions of what was received illegally-although I do not think people ever interpret that as illegal-he conducts himself differently. As long as we have a system under which one fellow can get away with receiving benefits improperly, other people will wonder why they should work when they can draw unemployment insurance benefits and con themselves into thinking they are entitled to them.
I feel that the officials of the Unemployment Insurance Commission are to be congratulated for being as alert as they were after the department indicated it wanted much stricter enforcement of the rules of the game. The rules of the game are now better because more justice is applied and more protection is available.
I should like the minister to give consideration to the fact that there are still a great many people who contribute to the unemployment insurance fund but who never draw any ben-

efits. There are a number of people who, because they have spent a large portion of their lives paying into this fund and have never received anything from it, want to draw benefits. They think that if they do not get something soon they will never get anything because they will soon be too old to qualify. It may take some work on the part of the minister's officials, but there should be a method worked out whereby a great many people could be provided an incentive so that they will not be tempted to draw benefits. If they knew there was something available in dollar terms at the end of their working life because they had not dipped into the fund, they might not be tempted to draw benefits for short periods of time.
The minister should undertake an examination of some type of incentive scheme which would provide special benefits to people who contribute to the fund year after year with no hope of ever drawing benefits. Their only satisfaction is the knowledge that they are helping their fellow workers who are involved in different types of work and find themselves unemployed from time to time.
Yesterday I made some comments about the hon. member for South Western Nova (Miss Campbell). I do not want to be unfair to the lady, but I find her approach to this legislation and to our area very negative. She indicated to this parliament and to the people of our province that our way of life is committed to unemployment insurance. I think there is a much more positive way to approach the unemployment problem in our area, and it is not by itemizing, as the hon. member did, the loss to the Atlantic provinces which will result from this legislation. At page 4497 of Hansard the hon. member said the following:
In terms of the loss of funds to the Atlantic provinces, if it is assumed that their loss is in proportion to the number of beneficiaries with 8 to 11 weeks in 1977- 11,496-then the loss would be between $63 million and $76 million in 1977.
In other words, the hon. member was saying to the people of Nova Scotia that because we are going to make the unemployment insurance fund an insurance fund rather than a welfare scheme, the government is going to take $63 million to $76 million out of the pockets of the people. I do not want to think that the people in my constituency have to look forward to unemployment insurance as their lifeline to security, three meals a day, and so forth.
I think the hon. member would be much better advised to propose schemes to the minister which would provide employment to those who would otherwise be unemployed between 7 and 11 weeks. But I say such employment should not be provided through Canada Works, LIP or similar programs. It can only be provided by allowing private enterprise to underpin our economy, by allowing it to work effectively. The government should not suck dollars out of the economy and spend them on public works projects. As it is, tax dollars are being taken out of the economy and used to provide jobs which taxes have eliminated.
I will not quote much more. The hon. member was crying the blues about her part of the country. She mentioned, as
March 31, 1977

reported on page 4497 of Hansard, that her area will lose $57,616 per week if this bill goes into effect. Then she said that if you multiply that figure by 52, there being 52 weeks in the year-a most profound observation-the result is $2,996,032. That much will be lost to her area. That may or may not be correct. I say that if the government puts in place proper programs to employ the unemployed, there will not be so many claimants drawing on the fund. And if they are forced to draw on the fund because they will have been employed for a long enough period they will qualify for benefits under the new scheme. The members of my area must try to make constructive proposals for eliminating unemployment. We should not encourage what I call the welfare syndrome; we should not encourage our people to rely on unemployment insurance benefits, welfare or any other benefits of that kind. I hope the hon. member will revise her philosophy on this bill and show some concern for people of her area. If she does, perhaps constructive steps will be taken in her area in the days ahead.
In conclusion, let me say that I hope the minister will be flexible in implementing the new proposals contained in this legislation. I say this bearing in mind present-day conditions, not because I oppose the objectives of the bill. The government, by having the Minister introduce the bill at this time, has not done anyone any favour. I only hope we shall be able to devise a scheme which will be workable in the long run, self-sustaining and help to eliminate some of the difficulties we have faced in the past.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO ESTABLISH DEPARTMENT OF EMPLOYMENT AND IMMIGRATION, ETC.
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, will the hon. member permit a question? I may have misunderstood the hon. member's comments but it seems to me he was somewhat inconsistent. I understood the hon. member to say that the unemployment insurance bill is departing from insurance principles. Then, near the end of his remarks, he suggested that we should depart even further from insurance principles by saying to those who would collect unemployment insurance, "If you do not collect unemployment insurance, we will set up a little fund for you." I wonder if the hon. member's suggestion would not involve an even further departure from the insurance principle.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO ESTABLISH DEPARTMENT OF EMPLOYMENT AND IMMIGRATION, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, with respect, no, I do not think so. Perhaps the hon. member did not understand me. I think that if we provide incentives for not drawing unemployment insurance, people who may be unemployed for a short period will not draw on the fund. Perhaps as an inducement we could provide a small payment. But in the end the government will save money since fewer people will try to collect from the fund. I suggest we could give the people who never draw money from the fund a little bonus as a reward.
Let me illustrate what I mean. The hon. member for Qu'Ap-pelle-Moose Mountain (Mr. Hamilton) told me of a school board in Saskatchewan which had tremendous difficulties with employees taking extensive sick leave. Every time a teacher stayed off sick, the board had to hire a substitute teacher, and this cost much money. In the end the board said to its employees, "If you do not take sick leave for a certain period,
Employment and Immigration
we will pay you a bonus." The scheme worked. Because of that incentive, the problem of sick leave was almost entirely eliminated. As it is now, many employees say from time to time, "Well, I have worked so many weeks now; it is time to draw a little benefit to get back some of the money paid in." That is the feeling of many who pay insurance premiums. I think the minister's officials should consider this idea. I think Dr. Clark, who prepared a report for the department several years ago, made a similar suggestion. Perhaps it is possible to conceive a scheme which will make people think twice before they avail themselves of benefits from the unemployment insurance fund. At present they do not think twice. Perhaps the minister may not think what I have said is a satisfactory explanation, but it is a suggestion.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO ESTABLISH DEPARTMENT OF EMPLOYMENT AND IMMIGRATION, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I shall keep my comments brief since I know a number of my colleagues wish to speak. First, I echo the sentiments of the hon. member who preceded me. I agree with what he said about the minister. I have the highest respect for the minister. I think he has made an honest attempt to design legislation in the best interests of all the people of this country.
I rise to speak on this bill with mixed feelings. Let me deal, first, with some of the good aspects of the legislation.

speakerposition: Deputy House Leader of the Official Opposition; Progressive Conservative Party Deputy House Leader
subsubtopic: MEASURE TO ESTABLISH DEPARTMENT OF EMPLOYMENT AND IMMIGRATION, ETC.
speechtext: That shouldn't take long.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO ESTABLISH DEPARTMENT OF EMPLOYMENT AND IMMIGRATION, ETC.
speechtext: I say this because, contrary to what some people have charged, not all parts of this legislation are completely bad.

speakerposition: Deputy House Leader of the Official Opposition; Progressive Conservative Party Deputy House Leader
subsubtopic: MEASURE TO ESTABLISH DEPARTMENT OF EMPLOYMENT AND IMMIGRATION, ETC.
speechtext: Which parts?

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO ESTABLISH DEPARTMENT OF EMPLOYMENT AND IMMIGRATION, ETC.
speechtext:
I say to the hon. member, "Take it easy." First let me say that the joining together of the two branches of the department is a good idea. I remember that I had the privilege in 1973 of spending two weeks in West Germany with other parliamentarians looking at the national employment service of that country. Without question, a one-stop shopping centre, so to speak, is a good idea and I agree with that aspect of the bill. I repeat, as I said before, that if the minister decentralizes the work of his office, once that union is complete he will make his organization more effective. I think smaller, regional offices under the new union will be a step forward. Another good aspect of the bill is the improvement in maternity benefits. I welcome another provision of the bill which will affect my riding. I am referring to that part of the bill which will allow one not to terminate a claim after working four weeks. Right now, if people claim work four weeks or more they must put in a new claim. That has caused a lot of hardship to people, particularly in the rural areas of my riding. Those people are often short-term claimants. This aspect of the bill will be good news to them. Nor can I disagree with the need to tighten the system across the country. There are parts of this country where the system needs to be tightened and where there is a great lobby to have the unemployment insurance system, as it obtains at the present time, considerably tightened.

March 31, 1977
Employment and Immigration
The controversial parts of this bill are the increase in the qualifying period from 8 to 12 weeks and the changes in the extending period. I realize there is a strong lobby for these things in many parts of the country. Many people are concerned with what they consider to be a rip-off of unemployment insurance. There is no doubt that in certain areas and in certain cases a rip-off is occurring. We must use all means within our power to ensure that does not happen.
I want to represent today, as is my responsibility and privilege to do in this House, a group of people who may be a minority in this country. They will be adversely affected by changes in this legislation. These people live in the rural parts of my constituency, particularly along the northeast coast of Newfoundland where there are not job alternatives. In certain parts of the country where there are job alternatives there is no question at all but that the act should be tightened along these lines. I want to put on record the feelings of these people. They may be a minority, but this party has always attempted, and attempted very well, to represent the feelings and positions of the minority groups in this country.
Much as this government has done to create jobs, and it has done more than any other government in the history of this country, much as we have put money into DREE and equalization grants across the country, LIP and Canada Works, there are still people in this country who cannot find alternative jobs. When this legislation comes into effect there will still be people in that position. They may be in a minority, but we have to think about and make provision for them. Where can we provide jobs for the people in the Atlantic area? They will jump at them. It is a myth that people are not prepared to work and would rather exist on unemployment insurance. All we have to do for evidence is look at the number of applications that come in for LIP and Canada Works. There are five or six times as many applications from my constituency as there is money that can be funded. People are looking for work in their own area. The work ethic is strong in Newfoundland and Labrador and, indeed, throughout the maritime area. People are looking for legitimate jobs. They will take them wherever they can find them. Look at the number leaving the Atlantic area, going to other parts of Canada, the continent and the world in search of jobs.
I have heard of people from the Atlantic area going to Ontario for a while, staying eight weeks, drawing unemployment insurance and going back home again. In the city of Toronto there are hundreds of thousands of Newfoundlanders who have gone there, stayed there, raised their families there and obtained permanent jobs there because they could not find them at home. It is not true that these people are taking advantage of the system. There are Newfoundlanders who have gone to Toronto, Hamilton, Galt, and many other areas seeking jobs because there are no jobs at home.
There are structural weaknesses in the economy of the Atlantic area. I realize that job creation is much better than just providing unemployment insurance. However, we are putting the cart before the horse. By creating jobs we will take

people off unemployment insurance automatically. Until such time as we can correct those structural weaknesses and create those jobs, let us not take away the only support that these people have at the present time. Let us not take away their integrity and self-respect. Let us not force them to accept welfare and for some people that would be the only alternative.
Must we have a rigid system in this country? Must we have a system that applies in the same way in every part of the country? This government recognizes regional differences in DREE, the provision of equalization grants and in the allocation of moneys under LIP and Canada Works. Can we not recognize these regional differences in applying these unemployment regulations? I want to put before hon. members the Greek figure of Procrustes, a man associated with Greek hostelry. He had a bed of one size. Every guest who came to the hostel had to fit the bed, no matter how big or how small he might be. If a man was too long, he chopped off his legs to fit the bed. If a man was too short, he elongated him to make him fit the bed. Up until the present time this Liberal government has not had a Procrustean philosophy. This government has had a policy which has recognized regional differences.
I make a strong plea that in this legislation we again recognize that there are regional differences in this country which have to be accounted for and for which provision must be made. If we are to have a strong country, we must allow for these regional differences. There is a debate now going on in this country. That debate concerns not only linguistic and cultural differences, but social and economic differences as well. I hope we can allow for those in this legislation.
Let me say again that the people in the Atlantic area would much prefer jobs to unemployment insurance. The evidence is there. However, let's not put the cart before the horse. There are areas in this country where the increase in the qualifying period from 8 to 12 weeks will be welcomed. There are other areas where it will hurt the minority groups and little people which this party has always attempted to defend.
It may be difficult to be liberal in this day and age when much of society is swinging to the right, but I say again that we have always tried to provide for the minorities in this country and have tried to give them a voice. I hope we can consider their plight at this time. I hope we can have an assurance from the minister that job creation will be in those areas most affected, or that the system will be flexible enough to accommodate the needs of various areas in this country, particularly the Atlantic area.
I want to put on record a telegram I received today from a member of the House of Assembly in my constituency. It expresses the feelings of many people in my constituency:
It is with regret that I feel compelled to convey to you my strong objections to your proposed changes in UIC regulations especially those that would increase the qualifying period for benefits from eight to 12 weeks. I am convinced that this increase in the qualifying period will bring undue hardship and economic suffering to many thousands of my fellow Newfoundlanders.
I will not read the whole telegram. There are areas of. the country that will be affected by this legislation. I hope we can
March 31, 1977

come up with a system that will make provision for people who have no alternative at the present time.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO ESTABLISH DEPARTMENT OF EMPLOYMENT AND IMMIGRATION, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as everyone knows, Bill C-27 is intended to amend the Unemployment Insurance Act, 1971. Unfortunately, this bill contains very few suggestions to provide the unemployed and those looking for jobs with a glimmer of hope to improve their situation. Members of parliament have received background papers and letters from different organizations with regard to the problems of unemployment insurance. Many have prepared excellent background papers. I wish to refer to one in particular, that of the Canadian Manufacturers' Association. It contains some very interesting points. I quote:
In the face of such substantially and demonstrably higher payroll costs one might ask, "Where would you locate a new plant to serve the North American market?" Even more to the point, for purposes of this discussion, "How long can we realistically expect to maintain existing jobs, let alone create new ones, when our costs are higher than the Americans?"
Now let's look at a specific social security program-unemployment insurance. Last year (1976) the total (state and federal) cost of U.S. unemployment insurance benefits was $15 billion. It caused an uproar in Congress because previously the annual cost in the U.S. (with ten times the Canadian population) had been between $3 and $4 billion!
In 1976 Canada's unemployment insurance cost almost $3.4 billion!!!
Despite higher unemployment rates in the U.S. throughout 1976, the cost of the U.S. program was approximately one-half that of the Canadian program whether viewed from the standpoint of dollars per person employed or as a percentage of GNP.
These are startling figures. When the United States can operate its program at half the cost, it shows there is something radically wrong in this country.
In light of the foregoing CMA intends to tell the house committee reviewing Bill C-27 that parliament, in the name of responsible government, has no alternative but to take steps to bring some of these comparative figures into line before even more jobs are driven out of Canada.
In this connection we propose to use charts to demonstrate those aspects of our unemployment insurance program which are badly out of line with the U.S.
One aspect of the Canadian program which cannot be quantified accurately is the rate of labour turnover. Studies by the U.I. Commission as well as an independent study by Simon Fraser University arrived at different estimates as to the percentage of unemployment which is induced by the disincentive features of our existing program. The important point is that, whatever the percentage, the studies agree that the existing program does induce unemployment and high labour turnover. Turnover rates of 200 to 300 per cent are reported by CMA members offering the highest wages in their communities and add to what economists refer to as "frictional" unemployment. The aggregate hiring costs and the extent to which this turnover inflates our unemployment rate cannot be measured by CMA and we will therefore not have charts to demonstrate these points.
They go on to say:
We shall, however, offer charts to the House committee on those points which are measurable. As an example we will point out that the average qualifying period in the U.S. is 25 weeks and that nowhere in the U.S. do they have a qualifying period as low as eight weeks, or even our proposed 14 weeks!
So when we suggest we are introducing a 12 week qualifying period we are certainly not being out of line or unjust in this country.
At the same time we will note that maximum benefits in Canada are $133 per week (with an automatic annual inflator), compared with an average maximum
Employment and Immigration
of $96 per week in the U.S. In some states benefits go as high as $130 but they also go as low as $60.
Of course that is one of the general complaints in Canada- that our benefits are far too generous. They are certainly not inducing people to look for work.
Similarly invidious comparisons appear when we examine benefit levels and duration of benefits.
Faced with this reality is it any wonder that U.S. interests are repatriating investment capital-and the jobs that go with it-to the U.S.? Is it a wonder that Canadian investment capital, and jobs, are going in the same direction?
It isn't easy for a politician to tell it like it is when, in fact, the truth hurts. But can responsible politicians do less than tell Canadians the truth in terms of the costs and effect of our current unemployment insurance program? Do they owe Canada anything less than these simple truths if we are to reverse the flight of jobs?
I should like to point out that we in the Conservative party called, in the last federal election, for a complete and independent review of the unemployment insurance scheme which is now costing us about one tenth of our whole budget. The size of the commission staff keeps increasing and there is every indication that this is not one of our better run corporations or government departments. It is certainly time that a complete overhaul was embarked upon and an independent inquiry conducted.
I should like to mention an incident which came to my attention in downtown Ottawa. A couple of weeks ago I was driving by the premises of a plumbing firm. There was a large outdoor sign near it, stating in huge letters "Full-time truck driver wanted". I cannot understand why any firm would need to put up a big billboard indicating they wanted a full-time truck driver. It would certainly suggest to me that the UIC was not doing its job properly, inasmuch as it would seem to have failed to find a truck driver for a plumbing firm in Ottawa.
A few days ago we received some propaganda from the Minister of Manpower and Immigration (Mr. Cullen). He sent members of parliament a note letting us know what Senator Humphrey had been doing in the United States. The note said:
Dear Colleague:
Senator Hubert H. Humphrey, Vice-Chairman of the Joint Economic Committee of the Congress of the United States, has recently written to me concerning youth employment programs in our respective countries.
Last January, Senator Humphrey introduced a comprehensive youth employment act in the United States Congress, and in February he used a great deal of information on Canadian programs as supportive evidence.
Well, Mr. Speaker, if the United States are going to rely on Canadian programs to cure their unemployment, their approach will certainly need to be changed. The Minister of Manpower and Immigration included with this letter a copy of the Congressional Record containing extracts from a speech by Senator Humphrey under the heading "How Canada attacks the youth unemployment problem." Well, Mr. Speaker, the minister and his colleagues may be attacking it, but they are certainly not knocking it down.
With regard to youth unemployment, the time has come for the government to place a special emphasis on the whole problem presented by young people who are unemployed.

March 31, 1977
Employment and Immigration
Young Canadians are the people hardest hit by the heartless economic policies of the Liberal regime.
How long can this country sustain a jobless rate among the young that in some areas amounts to 25 per cent or even more? Unemployment at any age is never pleasant but most people with a few years' experience have acquired some saleable skills. The perennial complaint is, and a legitimate one at that, employers want people with experience-but how can young people get it without finding that first job?
Young Canadians are caught in a long range pattern of diminishing career-orientated jobs. At the same time automation is slowly but surely eliminating employment.
In the 1960's governments told young people to stay in school and they would get jobs. They didn't! Now they are telling them to learn skills and they will get a good job. Another piece of Liberal propaganda.
Many young people who are employed are disenchanted and apathetic about their work. A negative attitude toward youth on the part of employers and older workers is one of the main reasons. Youthful disenchantment toward jobs can be traced to breakdown between expectation and reality.
Studies have indicated that young unemployed have tended to stay out of work longer than older people. Such figures are a clear indication that the government is shirking its responsibility to deal with this situation.
I should like to make a few comments on the need for a national apprenticeship system. I suggest the government should seriously consider this proposal. I notice that in today's Ottawa Journal a story appears in which the minister is interviewed. It is headed: "Tough-Talking Bud Cullen Finds Commons Irrelevant". Well, I think most Canadians, as well as members of the opposition, find his department most irrelevant when it comes to locating jobs for young Canadians. He also says that members of the opposition do not come up with many constructive proposals. I might point out to him that I come up with many constructive ideas in my speeches; I do not just stand here making negative speeches time and time again. The party to which I belong has always produced constructive proposals at election time. Indeed, my hon. friends have made a great many constructive speeches.
I intend to suggest that something should be established along the lines of a national apprenticeship system, so I shall certainly be proposing something constructive. Such a plan would provide the young with at least a chance in a working environment. The basic elements would be as follows: a qualifying period with a maximum of two years for those between the ages, say, of 19 and 25; no restriction to be placed on a field of work; pay to be better than UIC benefits, and tax incentives to be offered to participating employers.
I would also be in favour of a national work draft which would, by use of a lottery, absorb at least 10 per cent of the young people entering the job market for the first time. They could be employed in several ways, all of course productive and creative. The draft, by the way, would not be compulsory but rather one people could register with. These are, of course,

only suggestions meant to stimulate discussion, but the fact of the matter remains that thousands of young Canadians are out of work.
The Progressive Conservative party has been taking a serious look at the entire issue of student summer employment. All indications are that this summer will find more students out of work than during any previous summer. The facts also reveal that the dire situation facing students is largely the result of government indifference and the Liberals' lack of priority in this area. The facts are clear. Recent reports from Statistics Canada indicate that Canada has the highest rate of unemployment among young people ever recorded.
This government is breaking every record that it is possible to break in the world. I can give a number of other examples of records being broken, Mr. Speaker. Canada is now running the largest foreign debt in the western world. Our average wages in manufacturing are now the highest in the world, and our exports are dropping. We hold the world's record for hours lost per thousand workers due to labour disputes and strikes, losing five times as many man-days per thousand workers as Britain. Average wages in Canada last year increased by 14 per cent, nearly double the rate in the United States. Since 1972 our labour cost per unit of output has increased more than 50 per cent, compared to only 20 per cent in the United States, and our productivity also suffers in comparison. Our trade deficit on manufacturing last year was $10 billion. Our money supply, a chief cause of inflation, was up 22.8 per cent of the annual rate last month. No wonder we have high unemployment in Canada, Mr. Speaker, with a record like this.
In 1976 findings indicated that because of the general lack of jobs available to students, post-secondary students had to take jobs usually taken by graduating high school students. Therefore, as a result of this development, student unemployment rates increased. An even more alarming indication of the government's inability to grapple with or understand this problem is that Manpower's own participation survey-
