March 31, 1977
Veterans Affairs

This is the second notice of motion for the production of papers on the transfer of hospitals that I bring before the House requesting all pertinent material in the negotiations between the federal government and the provincial government concerned in the transfer of the Queen Mary Hospital veterans' wing in the province of Quebec.
My other motion on December 2 1976, had to do with the transfer of Westminster Hospital in London, Ontario. While anything I have to say on the hospital transfer would be repetitive-

speakerposition: Assistant Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Order, please. 1 ask members of the House to take their seats, please. I do not know whom to recognize as about a dozen members are standing.
Order!

Some of us should be put into veterans' hospitals. As I was saying, anything that I might have to say on hospital transfers would be repetitive. The main point I want to make is that it is ridiculous for the government to refuse to produce the papers, which only makes one suspicious of its intentions and of its sincerity. There is absolutely no need to refuse to produce the documents requested because, through some poking around in the department, through questions put to the minister in the House, through various telephone calls, and with the co-operation of departmental officials, I was able to gather together most of the information.
On March 28 I asked the minister about the status of the negotiations with regard to Queen Mary and St. Anne's hospitals. In his reply he said that negotiations are going on with the province of Quebec in accordance with government policy and that there is constant contact with veterans' organizations. He also said in his reply that he can give an assurance that veterans are cared for and that employees are protected.
This is the point of my motion. Why is it that the House of Commons, members of the Standing Committee on Veterans' Affairs, and indeed any member who has a veterans' hospital in his district, are denied the opportunity to perform their duty by offering advice and transmitting the assurance given by the minister to veterans and hospital staffs? All we hear from the minister is that everybody agrees, and yet about two weeks ago the chairman of the Hong Kong Veterans' Association, Mr. Charles Brady, wired the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) and the Minister of Veterans' Affairs (Mr. MacDonald), and sent copies of the wires to all members. I think I should read them into the record. The wire to the Prime Minister refers to his letter of January 17, 1973, regarding hospital transfers. It reads:
-today while at Queen Mary Veterans' Hospital Montreal was advised provincial government will make it a chronic care hospital after transfer. Veterans' rights for bed space will be denied which will be a first in DVA transfers. It is tragic that the government will not honour its federal policy to veterans. Veterans need more care now. We have to find out exactly what is going on. Confirm RSVP.
He also sent a wire to the minister which reads:
Your letter December 22, 1976, re hospital transfers, page 2. Re St. Anne's reads federal policy to guarantee no diminution of level of facilities for use of veterans. Was in touch with Queen Mary hospital today. Was advised provincial government will make it a chronic care hospital. Veterans' rights for bed space will be denied. This will be a first in DVA transfers. It is disturbing that the government will not honour and maintain its federal policy. Confirm details re Queen Mary transfer RSVP.
He also sent another wire which reads:
Today contacted Queen Mary Veterans' Hospital, which can be transferred to provincial government any day now. Was advised it would become a chronic care hospital means loss of jobs. More important this will be the first time in DVA transfers that veterans' rights for bed space will be denied. St. Anne's could follow the same course in 12 months, if we don't do something now. Veterans cannot permit these tragic developments to pass. Time for action is now. Recommend veterans' groups make joint representation before the Standing Committee on Veterans' Affairs and Minister MacDonald ... RSVP Hong Kong Veterans' Association of Canada.
Every time we ask the minister, as I said before, we are told that everything is fine, and yet before a hospital is transferred everyone else but the minister receives letters and telegrams of protest. As I said before, I ask in my motion why we are denied this information which we can receive anyway, to allow everyone here to assure veterans that the care which was promised will be given them? This was the commitment made by the Department of Veterans Affairs for many years.
The minister has made a number of visits to the Royal Jubilee Hospital. He has visited the veterans' pavilion there and heard concerned citizens and veterans' rights organizations express widespread dissatisfaction with regard to veterans, their dependants, and the wives of those who are supposed to be getting proper care in the veterans' pavilion at the Royal Jubilee. I have said many times that no one quarrels with the concept of transferring hospitals to non-departmental agencies due primarily to the trend indicating a need for more extended care rather than acute care, and due to the difficulty in keeping medical staff, for obvious reasons. However, I have also said that when the decision was made by the cabinet in 1963 to transfer veterans' hospitals, there was a lack of projection of the number of beds which should be provided. It has now been proved that we were right.
A report dated November, 1976, was given to me. It is a report by the treatment services division which shows the waiting period in hospitals already transferred to be up to 15 months. It also shows that in a hospital not yet transferred the waiting time is up to 18 months.
This has to do with a hospital which has not yet been transferred, Deer Lodge Hospital in Winnipeg. At Ste. Anne's hospital in the province of Quebec, which will eventually be under negotiation, there is a waiting period of up to 12 months, and the number on the waiting list totals 225. The lack of projection is emphasized by the example at the Royal Jubilee because of an increasing veteran population in Vancouver, which I will discuss later.

Mr. Speaker, I rise on a point of order. The hon. member for Humber-St. George's-St. Barbe (Mr. Mar-

March 31, 1977

shall) is giving figures, but I do not know where he gets this information.

For the information of the hon. member the figures come from the treatment services division. The assistant deputy minister is Dr. A. F. Jones, and the Figures come from a report on the various hospitals. This is an example of hon. members not knowing what is going on with regard to transfers. Through no fault of his own the chairman of the Standing Committee on Veterans Affairs is not getting this information. It could be received by everybody if this information were tabled. I will give the hon. member the correct information.
Another thing which is obvious is that the Department of Veterans Affairs is committed to ensuring the care of our aged veterans. I admit that the treatment services section and the hospital staffs are completely dedicated to veterans, but this dedication is lost in many cases as a result of transfers to non-departmental agencies. The non-departmental agencies have a different attitude. They are involved with civilian hospitals, if I can use that term, and the dedication is not the same because those agencies do not understand what is required for veterans. They cannot be expected to show the same feeling for veterans, but there is an obligation on the Department of Veterans Affairs to ensure care.
Let us look at what the paper on the hospital transfer program says. I want to quote from one of the paragraphs which indicates the following:
Where the transfer of a hospital from DVA to provincial authority has taken place, DVA reimburses the province for the care of pensionable disability cases, and pays premiums where required on behalf of veterans who are eligible for war veterans allowance. However, the treatment of all veterans (other than those requiring treatment for a pensionable disability) is now taken care of by the provincial hospital service in provincial hospitals; veterans do not receive priority.
An exception was made for the treatment of pensionable disability cases. In a directive on 9 December, 1963, Cabinet affirmed its intention that in any transfer, there should be a guarantee of unconditional priority use of beds for the treatment of veterans with service incurred disabilities, either in the transferred hospital or in some other hospital.
This is not happening, and that has proved to be the case after every transfer. This is shown in the list put out by the treatment services division of the Department of Veterans Affairs, which has all the facts and figures.
The Canadian Legion represents most of the 500,000 veterans of Canada, but there are many other veterans' organizations which are also concerned about hospitals, and they are not included in the consultations which take place. They find out after decisions are made and after mistakes, if any, are made.
At Ste. Anne's Hospital proper care is provided, and the number of beds which is needed is there. The purpose of this motion, past motions, and future motions is to focus attention on the fact that we as members of the Standing Committee on Veterans Affairs or any member of parliament should be able to find out what is going on and to have an input.
The following is what one national veterans' organization had to say:
Veterans Affairs
Veterans across Canada appear to be completely confused regarding the future of veterans' hospitals and the attendant matters of treatment and domiciliary care.
When the government's intention to transfer DVA hospitals to the control of other jurisdictions was announced in 1965, the matter seemed simple enough. Veterans were told that suitable arrangements would be made for treatment for pensioned conditions and that others who were entitled to treatment (e.g. war veterans recipients) would be looked after. A promise was made, as well, that there would be sufficient bed space for domiciliary care.
At that time, DVA officials gave the impression that these transfers would be carried out with despatch and the veteran would know precisely where he stood in regard to availability, to him, of medical facilities. We all know that this just did not happen-
I might add that this does not happen in every case, but it does happen in some.
-and some ten years later veterans in many areas do not know, from day-today, what provisions will be made for their medical treatment.
It is now 12 years later. This organization also had this to
say:
This situation is deplorable-
I would not use that strong a term, but the situation is doubtful.
-the government should clarify its policies regarding the transfer of DVA hospitals. We realize that, in many instances, the terms regarding such transfers are often being dictated by sources not under control of the Canadian government. This may cause undue delay. Notwithstanding, veterans are entitled to know what is happening to the institutions which were originally built for the purpose of providing medical care for them.
In accordance with the original announcement of 1965, veterans were to be consulted in regard to any transfer. The experience has been, in most instances, that the arrangements are in the last stages of completion and then the veterans' organizations are informed. It may be that the commitment to consult the veterans' organizations in advance is one which the government finds difficult to maintain-for the reason that negotiations regarding takeovers must usually be held in confidence. In any event, this hardly contributes to a feeling of security on the part of the veteran regarding treatment facilities.
It is our view that the entire matter of transfer of DVA hospitals should be reviewed by a committee comprised of officials of the Department of Veterans Affairs and the national veterans' organizations.
I would like to add to that the members of the Standing Committee on Veterans Affairs.
The terms of reference of such committee should be:
(1)	To determine what additional DVA hospital facilities should be transferred, if any; and
(2)	To arrive at a reasonable conclusion as to the number of domiciliary
care beds which should be available in each of the DVA districts.
We have reached a conclusion . .. that there is possibly some merit in further transfers.
I go along with that.
This would be clear, however, only if veterans' organizations could be made privy to essential information.
Our main concern is not with active treatment. We are aware that, in most areas, this will be available regardless of whether the treatment is given through a departmental institution or one under jurisdiction of some other agency.
It is the government's obligation to the aging veteran which seems to be the important question. We are aware that domiciliary care is looked upon by the department as a privilege rather than a right-and is dependent upon the availability of bed space. It is for this reason that it is essential that no further transfers be made-

March 31, 1977
Veterans Affairs
And this was the point of a number of motions I moved under Standing Order 43, which were not accepted. I continue quoting:
-unless there are guarantees that sufficient domiciliary care bed space will be retained; and, in fact, it may well be necessary for the government to do some 'back tracking' in certain areas where transfers have been made, and sufficient domiciliary care facilities have not been retained ...
There seems to be an attitude, on the part of some departmental officials, that veterans requiring domiciliary care are, in some respects, a community responsibility. Our organization contests this theory. The federal government has a responsibility to provide domiciliary care for the aging veteran. This is not a matter of right, at the moment, but it should be enshrined in the veterans charter, so that those veterans who prefer to spend their remaining years among their former comrades-in-arms in a good domiciliary care institution which can provide not only minimum medical care, blit also social and recreational amenities, can do so.
That is an important point. I say that many aging veterans, and some have reached the age of 104 I would have you know, want to spend the remaining years of their lives in their own environment. I think Canada owes them this, and I say this without wanting to sound dramatic or overly compassionate.
The helpful attitude which has been the hallmark of the doctors, nurses, and other staff of our better run DVA domiciliary care units in Canada represents something which cannot be found in most private facilities. It exists only in those veterans' institutions and it would be a sad reflection indeed if, because of shortsightedness at this stage, Canada were to fail to make sufficient provision in future for the domiciliary care facilities we know will be needed.
In order to give others an opportunity to speak I will refrain from making further comments but will reaffirm that we agree, for the reasons I have mentioned, with the concept of transfer of hospitals. It is difficult to get medical specialists to look after chronic, extended and domiciliary care cases. But there is that commitment. I think those who are concerned about veterans and have served for a number of years on the Veterans Affairs Committee should be allowed to provide some input. The parliamentary secretary opposite is one of the members of that committee. He is a learned, expert, and compassionate doctor. Nobody wants to oppose what the minister is trying to do. However, judging from the number of requests we have received, there is reason and justification enough for producing the papers requested and acceding to this request, made in the best interests of the veterans of Canada. It ought to be supported by members of this House and all those in Canada who are concerned about veterans.

speakeroldname: Mr. S. Victor Railton (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Veterans Affairs):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Veterans Affairs
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I shall try to answer some of the points made by the hon. member for Humber-St. George's-St. Barbe (Mr. Marshall). The hon. member requests the tabling of all correspondence, minutes of meetings, telegrams, contracts and agreements between the government and the province of Quebec having to do with the transfer of Queen Mary Hospital. Mr. Speaker, the minister cannot do this because our officials are still negotiating agreements with the provincial authorities. No definitive positions of accord

have been reached between the representatives of the provincial government and the Department of Veterans Affairs. There may be a little blue sky on the horizon. There are specific requirements which must be met in a number of important areas, and these requirements are presently under negotiation.
I think that it is misleading to talk about waiting lists. Mr. Speaker, no acutely ill person can wait one year for a hospital bed. Therefore I think the hon. member was referring to someone who needs a domiciliary or chronic care bed. These cases do not necessarily involve veterans who have been wounded or require treatment for their pensionable disability. Actually this question is of concern to the entire veterans' organization. We have at least 900,000 veterans in Canada.
The question has arisen whether the government promised domiciliary care to all veterans. Mr. Speaker, I do not think such a promise was ever made. Hospitals were never really designed to look after domiciliary care veterans. The hospitals we are transferring are excellent, acute treatment hospitals and should not be used for domiciliary care. They should be used by the sick people of the general population, which includes veterans. You may be sure that we shall look after the needs of veterans, but we must also make provision for the employees of hospitals and make sure they do not lose their employment.
That the government recognizes its moral responsibility is very evident. It is supposed to provide the best possible medical care for veterans who have a pensionable disability. Sometimes people do not agree with the way we are going about doing this, but we have a responsibility in this regard. I have met veterans all across Canada and can say, personally, that the great majority of veterans' organizations feel we are doing everything we should to look after veterans properly. Some people, of course, are always dissatisfied, no matter what we do.
It is now more than 30 years since World War II ended. We looked after our veterans awfully well when they returned. There were 40 veterans hospitals; we had to build special hospitals because there were not enough civilian hospitals to look after the men who needed specialized care. Lots of these men were severely wounded. The hospitals were filled with them. I had the opportunity to look after the men shortly after they were wounded, and know all about them. We looked after them devotedly and actively. They were given specialized care by doctors, and were often treated in specialized hospitals as well. However, over the years the number of veterans requiring active and acute care has decreased steadily. As beds became empty, they were made available to war veterans allowance recipients. Then, slowly but surely, the profile of the veteran patient changed.
May I ask how much time we have left, Mr. Speaker?

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Progressive Conservative Party

Order, please. There are about 15 minutes left.
March 31, 1977

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Veterans Affairs
speechtext:
The big question is, how are we to staff these hospitals? On this point I do not agree with the previous speaker. I do not think domiciliary care hospitals can be regarded in the same light as ordinary veterans hospitals which have looked after so many of the ill.
What does all this mean to veterans who will need hospitalization in the future? We hope that it will mean that the veteran will have available to him a range of services which will meet completely his needs at any given time. As a client who is an integral part of a modern community medical and hospital complex, a patient can call on all the resources of that complex.
I think I should defer to other hon. members who wish to speak. I could make a longer speech, to explain the situation, but am certain that other hon. members who wish to speak can do this very well.

Mr. Speaker, I rise to participate briefly in this debate. It is going to be brief because of a similar situation which is taking place in London, Ontario, where the transfer of the Westminster Hospital is in the negotiating stage with the province of Ontario. I understand that negotiations there are at a standstill because of some disagreements between the two parties. It would be helpful to all, veterans organizations in particular, if we knew precisely the nature of the difficulties and were provided with detailed information about the transfer terms. Veterans in all areas of Ontariq, particularly western Ontario, would then be in a better position to judge the rightness of the action being taken.
I agree with what has been said by my colleague, the hon. member for Humber-St. George's-St. Barbe (Mr. Marshall), that we are primarily concerned about the chronic and domiciliary care of those patients who are aging and are in acute need of this care. It is all very well to say that the care and special treatment provided in veterans hospitals has been adequate. It certainly has been. No one can find fault with that. However, we are now getting into another phase of care for veterans, that of chronic and domiciliary care. It is not too much to ask the minister and the department to take a good look at the need for providing this care which is perhaps just as great as the treatment care given in earlier years.
The Royal Canadian Legion has gone along with the policy of the department to transfer to other authorities. However, there are now some second thoughts, perhaps not by the Dominion Command but by Legion branches across the country. This is why it is essential that we should be privy to all information regarding the transfer of hospitals.
The Federation of British-Canadian Veterans of Canada requested that the federal government retain parts of Westminster Hospital. They are very specific about it, specifying that part south of Commissioners Road and that part east of Wellington Road. They want it retained as a memorial to those Canadians who have given their lives in defence of their
Veterans Affairs
country in order to provide the care about which I have been talking.
There are rumours that a company is interested in developing housing in the city of London. It is anxious to purchase some of the spacious grounds that surround Westminster, which is the pearl among all treatment hospitals in this country. To have this land used for such a purpose is completely wrong. We should know a little about that aspect of it as well.
Basic to the whole question we are talking about today, we need some guarantee that there will be priority for domiciliary care for our veterans. That has not been properly taken into account when the department has been negotiating. Officials have forecast a certain amount of bed space, but in every case they have fallen short. As a result, we have waiting lists of veterans wanting this type of care. They just cannot get it.
We need more information provided to members of parliament, particularly members of the Standing Committee on Veterans Affairs, in order to be in a better position to judge the correctness of representations now being made by Legion branches across the country which do not go along with the position taken by the Dominion Command.

Mr. Speaker, I willingly join in this debate on the motion of the hon. member for Humber-St. George's-St. Barbe (Mr. Marshall) to discuss this very important issue. We should actually talk about the condition which presents this issue, the problem of geriatrics, which we are getting into more than anything else. As all of us who belong to veterans organizations know we are a dwindling group. We are suddenly down to 900,000. We are now getting into a lot of problems, most of which evolve around age.
As former speakers have said, the veterans' organization has been well taken are of by the Department of Veterans Affairs and this government.
There are very specific conditions and guarantees written into these contracts. While the details might vary from province to province, the broad over-riding principles remain the same. In each hospital transfer, a specific number of beds must be guaranteed for pensioners for the treatment of their pensioned disabilities.
There must be assurances of adequate hospital accommodation for WVA recipients. At the same time the protection of employment for the existing DVA hospital staff must be negotiated. The veterans' organizations in each province are consulted because their input is very important to the success of the whole operation.
I am sure you can see from the things I have talked about that the government's position on striving for the best hospital care for disabled veterans is an on-going position, a continuing concern. We know that our disability pensioners are getting older, that they need primarily facilities for treatment of a chronic care nature. This is really the geriatric problem. It is a problem that is being very carefully discussed in Health and Welfare.

March 31, 1977
Veterans Affairs
One hon. member correctly asked the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Lalonde) how we are going to train staff and medical people to look after the geriatric problem? That is really the key to the issue of the transfers of these veterans' hospitals. We know that in the years ahead we will not be able to attract the staff to give them this modern, specialized care in existing veterans' hospitals. Therefore we have to get into the very involved and growing problem of training medical people in particular to look after not only the 55 years old as I am, but the older veterans, some of whom are sitting in this Chamber. There will be a real problem in getting medical staff to look after them, encouraging young doctors to become interested in the geriatric problem.
There are really two problems. Our Department of National Health and Welfare has a problem of providing for care, staff, and maintenance of these older people. It is unthinkable that we should allow these hospitals to deteriorate into second class institutions. We would not want that to happen. We have very carefully tried to avoid any consequence of that nature. We would like them to be suitable not only for the care of the aged but for any current condition that may arise.
All of the factors that went into the equation of establishing special hospitals for veterans have changed. Therefore a new equation must be worked out. We feel that the policy of transferring our hospitals to provincial jurisdiction, integrating them into the total community medical care complex, with built-in safeguards for the veterans who are our responsibility, and for our staff, is the best possible solution to the problem.
Let me take a moment to thank the staff who have worked so diligently over these 32 years. Some of them have been in veterans' hospitals for a long time. We should thank them for carefully ensuring that all those within the hospitals are mentally prepared for this transfer and are able to cope with it. Our staffs have always been careful to ensure that the patients know full well what is expected of them. This really comes up in the total community of health networks which I spoke about before, with the equation for establishing special hospitals having changed.
We feel the policy of transferring veterans' hospitals to provincial jurisdiction is completely justified. Let me elaborate on this, if I may. Veterans now have the option of going to the hospital of their choice and to the doctor of their choice. A veteran who needs medical attention no longer has to travel 50 miles from home to be looked after in a veterans' hospital. Now we have a policy under which veterans can go to their own family doctors, which makes it a lot easier for those who are not located near veterans' hospitals. Or, if he is not satisfied with his doctor, a veteran can choose another. He has the full range of modern laboratory facilities and specialized equipment at his command.
I am sure hon. members appreciate that the transfer of these hospitals is in no sense an abrogation of responsibility on the part of the government. Quite the reverse is true. The right of disabled veterans to the best hospital and medical care avail-

able is the principle on which all these agreements are negotiated. Every agreement provides that a guaranteed number of priority beds should be available for pensioned veterans; every agreement assures that the hospitalization needs of those veterans who are entitled to them are fully provided for. Every agreement assures that priority beds are provided for in hospitals approved by the department.
In addition, the rights of employees at the time of transfer are safeguarded. I suggest that a policy of transferring veterans' hospitals to provincial jurisdiction, integrating federal health care into a total community health context, is a responsible and progressive step forward. We owe a great debt of gratitude to the staff for facilitating the transfer to provincial authority. They are in a position to appreciate the ramifications of this policy. They will ensure the continuity of health care and services in this field. The Department of Veterans Affairs provides medical, dental and auxiliary care-

speakeroldname: Hon. Donald S. Macdonald (Minister of Finance) moved:
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
That this House approves in general the budgetary policy of the government.
He said: Mr. Speaker, over the past 18 months the government has directed much of its effort in economic policy to countering inflation. Canada has come a long way on the road to recovery from that inflation which first engulfed us in 1973. The rise of costs and prices disrupted many aspects of our economic life, and continues to do so. We must persist with our efforts to control it. The next section of the road back is beset with a number of hazards. The essential policy of this budget is to set forth a fiscal program to help guide the economy through these hazards.
One of the worst effects of inflation from which we continue to suffer is high unemployment. There never was any doubt that inflation would bring this result in its train. Our concern that inflation would produce worsening unemployment was a principal reason why the government embarked upon its strong anti-inflation policy.
Nor was there any doubt that the after-effects of inflation would be prolonged. We must not forget that fact now. Apart from all its adverse social results, inflation weakens the ability of our producers to compete at home and abroad. It also erodes the confidence so essential to the conduct of business and to investment in business capital. Without the restoration of confidence we will not generate the jobs we need. The task is the more difficult because our unemployment has been worsened by the failure of other economies to recover as rapidly as we had hoped.
One hazard of all this is that we will over-react and administer a shock of stimulus that is too strong to be absorbed without regenerating inflationary forces. What is required is stimulus of a degree that can be safely absorbed.
Another hazard is that we will succumb to the temptation to become more protectionist in the face of our impaired competitive position.That would surely be the wrong policy for a people so heavily dependent upon foreign trade. We are prepared to act, and have done so, in particular cases where domestic producers face serious injury. Such emergency action is consistent with our international commitments. But the government is convinced that the right policy over the longer term is to regain our competitive position by ensuring that our inflation is brought under control and to seek removal of barriers against our exports.
The Budget-Hon. Donald S. Macdonald
The decline in the value of the Canadian dollar that has occurred can be of benefit to our exporters and to those who compete with imports in our domestic markets. It is of crucial importance, however, that we do not erode this advantage by a resurgence of income increases that add to our costs. If we avoid that and press on to improve our relative cost position, then we shall benefit in our general standard of living from the freer world trading environment it is our policy to seek.
A third hazard is that the renewed price pressures coming from particular quarters will weaken our collective resolve to maintain the anti-inflation fight. Rates of increase of food prices declined sharply from mid-1975 to the end of 1976. But a combination of developments in the world has induced a new rise in food prices which is likely to continue for some time. World energy prices also continue to rise. We cannot shield ourselves from this hard fact. Canadians, like everyone else in the world, will have to accept still higher energy prices. In addition, the decline in the external value of the Canadian dollar is increasing the cost of our imports and pushing up domestic prices.
What is required is that we accept the inevitable impacts of these price increases upon our living standards, turn to substitutes where we can and reduce our demands for the higher-priced goods to the extent possible. Above all, we must avoid a renewed, self-defeating scramble for higher money incomes.
The prices and incomes program has served us well. We must continue to support it as long as necessary. We must press on with our consultations as to how responsibility can best be exercised in the determination of prices and incomes in the post-control period.
In developing a budget under these circumstances, two important constraints have had to be observed. The restraint of growth in the government's spending has been an integral part of our anti-inflation policies. The government believes such restraint is as important today as it was at the beginning of the program. By the control of existing expenditures, we are providing room for increases in spending that are most appropriate in the present circumstances. High priority has been attached to spending of the kind that will provide jobs for people.
The second constraint is the limit upon our ability to reduce taxes that is imposed by the need to restrict our demands upon the capital markets. The excess of our outlays over our receipts has to be financed. If it is financed by monetary expansion beyond that which is prudent, it defeats our purpose in containing inflation. If such an excess of outlays results in higher interest costs, the stimulus that we can impart to the economy is offset. Within this constraint we have found it possible to provide for further tax reductions in this budget.
Mr. Speaker, over the past four years, all the major economies of the industrial world have been confronted with infla-

March 31, 1977
The Budget-Hon. Donald S. Macdonald tion, recession and massive changes in international payments. Collectively they have made some progress in dealing with these difficult and stubborn problems. But persistent efforts will be needed over a long period of time.
In Canada, as I have said, the underlying momentum of inflation is slowing. With wage settlements coming down in line with the anti-inflation program, our unit labour costs- they key to our competitive position as a trading nation-are being brought under better control. At the same time, the real income of working Canadians has risen strongly.
Output in Canada grew rapidly early in 1976, but then the pace slackened here as elsewhere in the industrial world. As a result the number of new jobs created-209,000-was less than anticipated.
The most disturbing element in our performance has been the recent increase in unemployment. I am particularly troubled by the unemployment among the young people of this country. While the rate among adult men has remained well below 5 per cent, and is 7 per cent among adult women, it is above 14 per cent for young people. Moreover, the burden of unemployment has fallen much more heavily in the Atlantic Provinces and Quebec than elsewhere. The unemployment situation clearly requires not only some general measures of economic stimulus, but also specific initiatives directed at these structural problems.

Slack demand in 1976 led to a significant fall in profit margins. Many firms faced inadequate liquidity and rising debt-equity ratios. The low level of share prices made it difficult to raise additional funds in this form. All these factors contributed to the problem of financing the rapidly increasing costs of new investment projects.
Economic growth in 1976 was led by consumer demand and housing construction while government expenditure on goods and services grew more slowly. Real business investment actually declined despite strength in the energy field. We need renewed growth of business investment and a continuing improvement in exports to create jobs and lay the basis for sustained growth in the future.
The deficit in our balance of payments has increased in recent years, partly as a result of the deeper recession in other countries, partly from our rising bill for interest, dividends_and foreign travel, and from our shrinking energy surplus. But it is also the result of the difficulties our own inflation has created for Canadian producers in competing at home and abroad.
The recent decline in the Canadian dollar reflects lower interest rates in Canada, but it also reflects a sense of uncertainty about Canada's future among foreign investors. The decline will help to offset the higher costs incurred by Canadian firms. It will provide them with new opportunities to compete. These benefits are ours to seize, but only if we keep our domestic costs and prices firmly in check. The immediate impact of a lower dollar is to increase the prices of goods and services to Canadian consumers. If this leads Canadians to demand higher money incomes, the opportunity for a lasting

improvement will be lost. Further depreciation would then be needed to offset still higher costs. We must avoid this downward spiral.

Our goals are clear.
Our first objective must be to maintain the underlying trend to lower inflation.
Our second objective must be to encourage a steady and non-inflationary growth in the economy, in order to provide jobs and reduce unemployment.
I want to emphasize that the federal government recognizes and accepts its responsibility for action to help achieve these goals. But responsibility for the economy rests on others as well. Both political and economic power are widely dispersed in this country, reflecting Canada's diversities and protecting our fundamental liberties. All those who share power also share the responsibility that goes with it for the attainment of our economic goals.
This is well illustrated in the recent record of economic and fiscal cooperation between the federal and provincial governments. That record provides reassuring evidence of the continuity and flexibility of our Confederation while contributing directly to the solution of our economic problems.
Responsibility also rests with our business leaders. It is private firms which employ most of our workers, make most of the investment decisions in our economy, and develop the markets and the new technologies that enhance our standard of living.
An important responsibility also rests with the leadership of the labour movement at every level in this country, for jobs are at stake. Indeed, all Canadians share the responsibility for setting prices, wages and other incomes so as not to impair our opportunities for employment.
We set out in the discussion paper entitled The Way Ahead our views on how responsibility will have to be shared in the post-control society. We will realize the full economic potential of this country only if we develop a greater understanding of what we can realistically hope to achieve.
Mr. Speaker, I want to refer to five areas of public policy at this time, before I outline the specific measures proposed in this budget.

First, Mr. Speaker, energy. We no longer have ready and assured access to cheap energy supplies at home or abroad. In these new circumstances our objectives must be to increase our domestic supplies and to cut our energy demands. Restraint on the price of domestic oil and subsidies on imported oil can provide only temporary assistance to consumers, to provide time to adjust to the new realities. This spring, we will have to set the amount of the next price increase. Our challenge will
March 31, 1977

be to achieve a balance between longer-term energy objectives and the capacity of the economy to absorb further price increases at a time when we are facing unemployment, inflation, and severe international competition.
We will press on with our policy of developing energy supplies. But we must all develop better conservation practices. Canadians must face up to the prospect of higher prices. While it would be unwise to pay more than others do for oil and gas, it would be imprudent to expect that for long we can pay less. The best way for Canadian consumers to protect themselves against higher energy prices is to use less energy.

A second major policy area concerns the controls over prices and incomes. They have helped to bring down the rate of inflation, but their job is not yet done.
If controls were suddenly removed now, there is a danger that rates of cost and price increase would begin to escalate again. This would put in jeopardy the sustainable growth of output and employment. The federal government is not prepared to let that happen.
Mandatory controls over prices and incomes, however, cannot become a permanent feature of the economic life of this country. We need to create the conditions in which controls can be phased out without interrupting progress towards our economic goals.
We have advanced a number of options for decontrol and they have been widely discussed. The government believes that the best approach would be the phased approach based upon the timing of pay agreements and fiscal years. This is generally favoured by the provincial governments. It will be described in full in a discussion paper to be issued in the near future. The paper will also make proposals for a post-control monitoring agency, and suggest structural improvements in the economy. Included here will be a discussion of labour-management relations and public sector compensation policy. The paper will outline proposals for consultation between the government and the provinces, and business, labour and other interest groups. The objective will be to reach the broadest possible understanding of action needed to keep inflation coming down during the process of decontrol and in the post-control period.
Within this framework, there will be a particular need to consider a possible date for beginning the decontrol process. On the basis of all the factors at work, the government believes that a starting date prior to the second anniversary of the program on October 14, 1977 would not be feasible or desirable. A recent initiative on the part of business and labour groups, however, has raised the prospect of sufficient support emerging for a program of voluntary restraint as to warrant consideration of a somewhat earlier date. That could affect the question of timing. This prospect will be fully explored in the further round of consultations intended to follow the publication of the discussion paper. In the meantime, I advise all parties to proceed with wage and price determination in the
The Budget-Hon. Donald S. Macdonald expectation that controls will continue in effect for some time unless replaced by firm understandings which produce similar results. There is no room for any expectation that a time is coming when inflationary claims upon the national income can once again be made.

A third important policy area is job creation.
We have given high priority to direct job creation programs, especially for young people and in regions of highest unemployment.
The employment strategy featuring the major new programs of Canada Works and Young Canada Works has already been launched. Their impact will build up rapidly through the summer and into next winter. We have had a good response from the first call for proposals from public and private groups. This means that jobs will be created quickly. I wish to announce a $100 million expansion of our job-creating programs to boost employment further, where it is most needed. This expanded $458 million commitment for 1977-78 will create 600,000 man-months of employment. It will have significant impact in reducing the number of unemployed. My colleague, the Minister of Manpower and Immigration (Mr. Cullen), will be announcing details in the budget debate.

The fourth policy area is the goverment's continuing program of expenditure control.
We are now seeing the solid results of our commitment two years ago to get government expenditure growth below the growth rate of GNP. Our expenditures for the fiscal year just concluding are estimated at some $750 million less than the forecast contained in the budget of last May.
Our target for outlays in 1977-78 is $44,450 million, or $650 million less than the expenditure plan announced last month by the President of the Treasury Board. Part of this $650 million saving is a reduction in the reserves for Supplementary Estimates to make room for the tax reductions I am announcing tonight. Part is due to general success of the restraint policy, which is bearing down on every department of government.
On a fully comparable basis, expenditures in 1977-78 will be about 9.8 per cent higher than in the year just ending. That rate is lower than the expected growth of GNP and lower than the 11 per cent increase predicted in the last budget. This means, of course, that many useful and desirable programs are having to be delayed or curtailed.
Finally, Mr. Speaker, a fifth broad area of government action is monetary and fiscal policy.

March 31, 1977
The Budget-Hon. Donald S. Macdonald
The essential task of both monetary and fiscal policy in present circumstances is to encourage a growth of demand consistent with the expansion of employment and the winding down of inflation. In the case of monetary policy, it is the strategy of the Bank of Canada progressively to moderate the growth of the money supply. While the overall fiscal strategy has not been formulated in terms of a numerical guideline, here too the advantages of avoiding wide swings in the stance of policy are recognized. For some time, our policy has entailed a sizeable deficit. As the slack in the economy is taken up, the deficit will be reduced. However, to attempt to cut deficits too soon would threaten the recovery. Indeed, with present levels of unemployment, further stimulus is required.
In considering the extent of this further stimulus I have kept in mind the interrelated objectives we have set for ourselves. We cannot pursue rapid growth at the expense of more inflation and a worse balance of payments situation.
I have also been anxious to avoid placing too much pressure on the capital markets. This is to be avoided when we are seeking to encourage new private investment, and when other borrowers may be looking to the domestic capital market for an increasing portion of their financing needs.
In considering the type of fiscal stimulus to be provided, my starting point has been the commitment to expenditure restraint. Within this restraint we have been able to allocate further resources to creation of new jobs. Beyond that, we have turned to the reduction of taxes.

The measures proposed in this budget will create employment, encourage investment and foster regional growth. They will improve the equity market and improve the cash flow of business as sources of funds for expansion. They will give more help to small business and venture enterprises. They will help sustain consumer spending and provide further tax relief, particularly to Canadians with modest incomes. All of these measures will lead to more jobs.

I wish to announce a series of measures with respect to capital investment and regional growth.
Since 1975 the 5 per cent investment tax credit has proved to be an important incentive supporting our manufacturing and resource industries. I propose that the credit, due to expire June 30, be extended for an additional three years. Also the credit will be expanded in two important ways.
First, recognizing the importance of maintaining a vigorous research effort in Canada, I propose that capital and operating expenditures on scientific research and development be eligible for the credit.
Second, the credit will be increased in slower-growth regions designated under the Regional Development Incentives Act. In
£Mr. Macdonald (Rosedale).]
Saskatchewan, Manitoba, Northern Ontario and all designated regions in Quebec other than the Gaspe the rate of the credit will be raised to 7 Vi per cent. In the Atlantic Provinces and the Gaspe region the rate will be raised to 10 per cent.
In addition, the budget contains tax incentives directed toward increased exploration for oil and gas in frontier areas and toward improvements in rail transport facilities, particularly for the movement of grain and coal in Western Canada.

I am proposing further action to assist the financing of business investment. One of my particular concerns is the financing of investment through new equity issues. The market for such issues has not been very receptive in recent years. Moreover the equity base of many corporations has been reduced to a level which does not permit the further borrowing needed for business expansion.
I would like to propose therefore a major increase in the dividend tax credit. Starting January 1, 1978, dividends received from taxable Canadian corporations will be grossed-up by one half, as opposed to one third currently, and taxpayers will be allowed to claim against their tax a credit equal to this higher amount.
This will provide benefits in a progressive manner and make it more attractive for investors in all income brackets to participate in the equity market.
The increase in the dividend tax credit, and the maturing of the capital gains tax introduced in 1972, make it possible to abandon many of the complex rules designed to prevent surplus stripping, that is, the avoidance of tax on tjie distribution of corporate surplus. The present rules very often hamper constructive business reorganization and expansion. The rules will be eliminated or greatly simplified. Efficiency of business operation should be improved through the removal of artificial impediments to decision-making. It will be particularly beneficial to small business.
Other measures designed to improve the equity and financial markets will double the amount of capital losses which a taxpayer can set off against other income, and include capital gains in the present $1,000 exemption for interest and dividends. As well, stock dividends received from publicly listed corporations will not be taxed until disposed of, and then only at capital gains rates. Finally, the exemption from non-resident withholding tax for interest on government and long-term corporate bonds will be extended to the end of 1982.
Many concerns have been expressed about the effects of inflation in distorting the measurement of income reported on financial statements. We are co-operating with a number of groups in a search for a comprehensive inflation accounting system. Consideration of any comprehensive tax measures in this area should await the results of this work. However, the liquidity problems facing business are urgent and require an immediate response.
March 31, 1977

I am proposing at this time a deduction in calculating business income each year of 3 per cent of the opening value of qualifying inventories. The adjustment will be allowed for fiscal periods which commence after December 31, 1976, and will be available to both incorporated and unincorporated business.
This measure will provide tax relief of $300 million a year and enhance the flow of internally generated funds available for business expansion. It will be simple to use and require no fundamental change in accounting practices.
[ Translation]

Mr. Speaker, the government attaches great importance to the contribution small business makes to the Canadian economy. The venture capital review I announced in the last budget was devoted in part to the search for solutions to the financing problems of small business. This analysis revealed that no single tax measure could resolve them. Indeed, many of the problems of the small businessman are a part of the larger problem to which the measures announced earlier are directed. Substantial benefits will flow to small business from the proposals for the extension and increase of the investment tax credit, the increase in the dividend tax credit, the inventory adjustment and the other measures directed towards investment. But we can do more.
A particular problem for small business is the difficulty of matching higher salaries offered by larger enterprises. I propose to introduce a special tax treatment for stock option plans established for employees of Canadian-controlled private companies. The difference between the option price paid for the shares and their sale proceeds will be taxed as a capital gain and then only when the shares are disposed of. This will permit a company to reimburse its employees in a way that does not impair its working capital.
A serious impediment to venture capital investment is tax uncertainty. Certain investors face the possibility that their gains will be taxed fully as ordinary income rather than as a capital gain. Provision will be made for ordinary taxpayers to protect themselves from this risk.
A question which has been much discussed in past budget debates has been the handling of capital gains, particularly with respect to farm and small business properties.
When a commercial business is sold in the course of a move from the centre of a city, or when a farmer sells his farm and buys another, any capital gain is now subject to tax, even if the funds received are used to purchase similar assets in the same business. Tax will be deferred on any capital gain that arises from such voluntary sales after tonight to the extent that the proceeds are reinvested in similar assets.
Other measures of interest to the small businessman will include a relaxation of rules dealing with taxation of intercor-
The Budget-Hon. Donald S. Macdonald porate dividends, and measures relating to conversion to the metric system.

Turning to personal income taxes, a series of steps in recent months has improved the disposable income of Canadians. These have included the reduction in personal income taxes as a result of indexation and the reduction of unemployment insurance contribution rates, I believe we need further action to sustain personal expenditure and to provide some relief to Canadians who are particularly affected by higher prices of necessities.

First, I propose to enrich the existing credit against federal tax. The rate of the credit was recently changed from 8 per cent to 9 per cent as a result of the new fiscal arrangements with the provinces. The maximum credit is $500 per taxpayer and the minimum of $200 ensures that the greater benefit from the credit goes to taxpayers of modest incomes.
For the 1977 and subsequent tax years, taxpayers will be allowed to claim an additional credit of up to $50 for each dependent child under 18 years of age resident in Canada.
For example, a taxpayer with two children, whose current tax credit is $350, will be able to claim a full additional credit of $100. The limit of $500 will continue to apply, so that most of the benefit will be reserved for taxpayers with larger families and modest incomes. This measure is estimated to save taxpayers $275 million for the 1977 taxation year.
[ Translation]

A further major income tax reduction will benefit millions of working Canadians. The employment expense allowance is now established at 3 per cent of wage and salary income with a maximum deduction of $150. The limit will be increased to $250 effective for 1977 and subsequent years. This measure is estimated to reduce federal taxes by $ 115 million this year.
The combined effect of these two measures will be to eliminate completely the federal tax on married taxpayers with two children and earnings of less than $7,360. The comparable income level for a family with four children is $8,295.
These measures will make a tangible contribution to the personal disposable incomes of many Canadians.

RHOSPs
More than 400,000 Canadians have established Registered Home Ownership Savings Plans. These plans help taxpayers accumulate savings for the purchase of a home. However, the rules have been criticized for allowing families to contribute to a RHOSP as it is commonly called, even though they currently own a home or have no intention of acquiring one. I propose

March 31, 1977
The Budget-Hon. Donald S. Macdonald changes to prevent misuse of the plan. A taxpayer will not be permitted to make a contribution to a RHOSP if the spouse with whom the taxpayer is living already owns a home. Home furnishings will be excluded after this year from property eligible for RHOSP funds. Several relieving changes will be introduced to deal with particular problems that taxpayers have experienced with RHOSPs.

A number of other changes deal with structural problems in the income tax and the sales tax. In order to close a loophole in the income tax, there will be a change in the rules relating to Registered Retirement Savings Plans established for a spouse. There will be important changes in the taxation of life insurance companies and policyholders. Also, starting January 1, 1978 the rate of interest applied to refunds and late payments of tax will be increased.
In the sales tax the exemption for small manufacturers will be increased from $3,000 to $10,000. It is also our intention to exempt certain producers of craft products which are of significance to Canadian culture and heritage. Consultation with the crafts industry will be necessary before determining which groups will be exempted. Also, some additional energy conserving items will be exempted.
Finally, I want to refer to the Discussion Paper on Federal Sales and Excise Taxation. The issue here is whether the tax should be shifted from the manufacturer's level to the wholesale level. The matter requires further consideration. The report of the Commodity Tax Review group will be tabled shortly in the House. I have asked the President of the Privy Council to refer the report to an appropriate standing committee of the House for its assessment.

I come now to tariffs. I am proposing to extend for another year most of the current temporary reductions on a wide range of consumer products. The reductions were first made in 1973 in order to moderate upward pressures on prices and they were scheduled to expire on June 30.
I am also proposing to implement certain tariff concessions for imports from developing countries. These result from discussions held in Geneva during the multilateral trade negotiations. The purpose was to see if something could be done for products of special interest to developing countries in advance of the completion of the negotiations.
I would like to mention two other tariff changes.
First, I propose that the 2'h per cent British Preferential rate be withdrawn on certain machinery and related equipment imported from Britain and Ireland. This action is necessary because of serious difficulties facing Canadian manufacturers. These goods will become subject to the 15 per cent Most-Favoured-Nation rate immediately. Second, I am proposing to restrict the free entry accorded goods imported by Canadians returning from extended periods of residence

abroad. In order to prevent abuse, free entry in future will be limited to articles valued individually at $7,500 or less.
I also intend to ask the Tariff Board to study the coverage of two tariff matters upon which I have received many representations. The first is the item which provides duty-free entry for a wide range of goods imported by or for public hospitals and religious, educational and scientific institutions. The second reference relates to the treatment accorded to hobby equipment, antiques and other collectors' items.
Finally, in principle, I favour allowing recognized ethno-cultural groups to import traditional costumes free of duty. However, we need more time to consider the precise scope of any provision and we will be consulting with interested parties.
Oh, oh!
As the President of the Privy Council (Mr. MacEachen) points out, if we import kilts, he will be the first person to be consulted on this question.

Mr. Speaker, I am confident that the measures contained in this budget will help to quicken the pace of our economic recovery. Consumer spending will be sustained and investment stimulated. With renewed growth in the economies of our trading partners, we can expect a further improvement in our trade balance and a reduction in our current account deficit. Output in Canada will begin to rise again at the annual rate of 5 per cent or more needed to bring down the rate of unemployment. Given the time lags involved, this may not happen at once, but the rate of growth is expected to pick up during the course of the year.
For 1977 as a whole, the gross national product is likely to be about 4 per cent or more higher in volume and 11 per cent higher in value than in 1976. Employment is expected to be about 150,000 higher on average this year than last, but the increase between late 1976 and late 1977 could be as high as
250,000	jobs.
The proposals in this budget will reduce the federal taxes of Canadian individuals and corporations by $1.17 billion in the fiscal year 1977-78. This comes on top of the reduction of $900 million in federal personal income tax resulting from indexation and the quarter of a billion reduction in unemployment insurance premiums.
I now estimate that our financial requirements excluding foreign exchange will amount to $5.4 billion in 1976-77. They are forecast to increase to $6.4 billion in 1977-78. The deficit on the National Accounts basis is expected to rise from $4.5 billion to $5.7 billion.
Mr. Speaker, I would like to table the usual supplementary tables on the government's accounts and ask that they be appended to today's Hansard.

To sum up. We in Canada are not alone in struggling with the difficult task of bringing down the rate of inflation, restoring high levels of output and employment, and improving our balance of payments. From an international perspective, the performance of the Canadian economy, though far from satisfactory, has remained among the top three or four of the world's industrial nations. The incomes of Canadians have continued to grow, in real terms, faster than almost any other country. The program launched in October, 1975, is succeeding in bringing down the rate of inflation and checking the erosion of our competitive position. But recovery from the excesses of inflation is unavoidably slow, because the damage wrought continues to emerge well after inflation has begun to recede.
We have been fortunate that the majority of Canadians, deeply worried by inflation, have supported and co-operated with the government in its general anti-inflation policies. The controls program in particular has continued to command their support, despite the objections raised against it. But the months ahead will be a severe test, as unavoidable increases in prices of food and energy and the impacts of the decline in the exchange rate make themselves felt. These impacts cannot help but slow the gains in average real incomes. It will be crucially important for us all to accept this hard reality, continue to moderate our income demands, and persevere in the effort to beat inflation.
At the same time the pause in the economic recovery and the rise in unemployment has posed a severe problem. Clearly the economy needs stimulus. The budget seeks to provide it in the form and in the degree that will do the most good. Measures are proposed to increase the total demand for goods
The Budget-Mr. Stevens
and services, expand direct job creation, encourage investment and risk-taking on a national basis, and strengthen regional growth.
We have arrived at a stage in the evolution of our program when the temptation to seek quick and easy solutions will be great. We will be urged to spend our way out of our problems, to provide even greater stimulus, to provide protection against the realities of international competition and to withdraw controls before their job is done. These temptations must be resisted if we are to restore the confidence of Canadians and others in the future of our economy and achieve our economic and social goals.
Hear, hear!

Mr. Speaker, the Minister of Finance (Mr. Macdonald) has spoken and we have this shocking document before us. Before the Minister of Finance spoke, the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) spoke. Ten days ago the Prime Minister told some startled university students that if they were dissatisfied with job opportunities in Canada they should go to another country.
Shame!
Clearly the Minister of Finance got the message, judging from his budget tonight. The budget in effect proposes one million unemployed in Canada this year and next year.
Shame!

This Minister of Finance apparently has given up full employment budgeting and has substituted one million unemployed budgeting in its place. To those Canadians who say they do not like that kind of budgeting, to use the Prime Minister's words, find another country.
The budget says 150,000 jobs will be created this year, but the labour force is going to go up by 225,000. There will be
225.000	more people looking for work this year. Clearly the budget anticipates 75,000 more people being added to the
932.000	people now out of work.
Shame!

In last year's budget the administration said it was relying on foreign countries, the United States in particular, to provide our growth. This year the administration is going one better. Not only are they relying on friendly countries to provide our growth but the Prime Minister suggests that those same friendly neighbours should provide homes for our jobless. It would appear that the administration is virtually giving up.
At one time we were told by the government that growth was slow here because it was slow in other countries. Now it is suggested we should go to those same other countries to seek out jobs. What a pathetic attitude. Given the privilege of governing the people, this administration tells the people to go

March 31, 1977
The Budget-Mr. Stevens
to other countries to get work. It is incapable of providing an economic climate which would ensure jobs for our people, and the budget will do nothing of a meaningful nature to rectify this situation.
In that respect they talk of creating 600,000 man months of work. I wonder why they did not figure it out: how many man minutes of work would that be? Let us not be too confused. In effect they have said they feel the job creation program might produce 50,000 jobs this year. Confidence has been shattered by the Prime Minister's musings in the past. It has been shattered by a cabinet which does not have the intent, the will, or the knowledge necessary to restore a vital economy. They, the supposed servants of the people, have one answer to those who are unemployed: if you don't like it, get out of the country. To be more explicit, as the Prime Minister told an audience in Toronto, "My heart does not bleed for you." That is great news for the unemployed fishermen in the maritimes or on the Pacific coast, or for the miner looking for work in northern Canada. It is a brilliant solution for the 32,000 university graduates who cannot find work, or for the 200 lawyers who recently graduated in Ontario and have no jobs.
Oh, oh!

In our five eastern provinces, which are burdened with 45 per cent of our unemployment and where 80 per cent of the increase in unemployment has occurred in the last year, imagine how the jobless feel when they hear about this budget. Imagine the audacity of the Prime Minister, who holds himself out as the person best qualified to unite this country.
There is little in the budget for those who are looking for reasonably priced housing. There is virtually nothing in it to promote conservation. Granted, the minister is allowing wood stoves to be exempted from sales tax. But no effort has been made to remove double taxation of oil and gas producers. They are still expected to pay income tax on income not received but paid as royalties to provinces.
That is not all. Where are the meaningful tax cuts for the average family? Where is there recognition that under this government the tax load upon Canadian families has increased from 12.9 per cent to 18.6 per cent of their total income? Where is there recognition of the fact that Canadians, for the first time in history, now pay more in personal income tax than on any other item-more than they spend on housing or on food, and seven times more than they pay for medical care?
Because we are paying for that!

In the budget we have before us, the take of the government in Ottawa from individual taxpayers goes up by another 16 per cent if it is expressed on a basis consistent with last year.
Then there is the question of inflation. We are told the government is following a program of gradualism. Try to put gradualism in the bank. Explain to the housewife, as she watches prices jump month by month, that she should not worry, because gradualism, to use the government's term, is

working. Judging from this budget gradualism will continue, but it is certain prices will rise.
The government gives $650 million to stimulate business. But I can assure you, Mr. Speaker, that other measures in the budget, including the determination of ministers opposite to leave the controls in position, will more than counteract any stimulative effect they feel they may get from the money they are giving to business.
Where is the restraint of which we have heard so much? We recall the Prime Minister's quip that we are all living beyond our means. But who are living more beyond their means than the government? Since 1971 the total take from the GNP by governments in Canada has risen from 38 per cent to 43 per cent, and of that increase 80 per cent is at the federal government level.
The Prime Minister has said we are living too high off the hog. Let me assure him that nobody is living better than he is. He is getting the prize cuts!
Oh!

Based on the spending figures in this budget, if the administration had abided by its own spending guidelines in the past two years, federal spending would be less by $1.3 billion. That amounts to more than $100 per taxpayer in Canada. And they have resulted in the administration needing $6.3 billion this year to cover its cash requirements. Mr. Speaker, that $100 is, in effect, the amount of which the government has cheated the average taxpayer by its spending plans this year.
The answer given by the government to those who seek jobs is very simple: leave the country. When asked about inflation, they say it is caused by the weather or by some foreigner. When government restraint is requested, it is clear they prefer to leave that to the provinces. As for tax cuts, they shout: "Who needs them-we are living beyond our means anyway." The government's answer to the loss of export sales is: who cares-who needs to sell abroad if you can borrow abroad?
Oh, oh!

And as to business, this government cannot make up their mind whether it is better to continue attacking business or to ignore it. In the meantime they believe there should be controls. In the meantime they are confident more regulation of all of us is necessary, and some day they will squeeze an increase through for those favourite senior civil servants who the Prime Minister feels are underpaid at $66,000 per year and need $70,000. But, Mr. Speaker, more about all this later.
I move, seconded by the hon. member for Halifax (Mr. Stanfield):
That the debate be now adjourned.
